about: Fablebook brand data, version 2.0. Every rule in the brand book as structured data; American English. This edition defines no logo animation and no sound.
name: Fablebook

revisions.changes: Tenth pass, after the owner’s glance at the whole book: on the markers page, “What each means” now has one clear hierarchy, with the group headings Coverage and Preview set larger than the marker names under them and each meaning in the quiet color; the rest was read and left as it was.

Ninth pass, after the owner’s read of the whole book: “UI catalog” is the one name for Fablebook and the part you open (the descriptor is “A UI catalog for Phoenix LiveView”); “case” replaces “situation”, so a scenario is one screen in one case; Edited is a round outlined pill listed apart from the two coverage marks, Gap and Waived; the voice is “Plain”, with a plain-to-lively dial; moving between scenarios is instant and a component’s own animation plays as the app defines it; the type, hierarchy, coverage, README and docs, Hex and tab pages are realigned on one grid; the sample app cards have even spacing above their buttons; the terminal coverage output is an aligned table with “gap” in brick and “waived” in slate; the themes page drops its slogan line.

Eighth pass, after the owner’s read of the idea, messaging, presence and marker pages: the pitch is shorter; the first pillar shows each screen in situations such as a first visit, nothing there yet and form validation errors, with clearly named scenarios; a scenario is one screen in one situation, and the idea page says so with an example; the three markers are described briefly; the clear-space page says what the mark can be mistaken for; the favicon page is laid out as three cuts, the tile and the browser tab.

Seventh pass, after the owner’s read of the values: the values now state what Fablebook does instead of instructing the reader (“Previews your real UI”, “Names each scenario by the situation it shows”, “Says which screens are covered”), with “Gap” and “Waived” in quotes; the Yours value and the third messaging pillar say your user flows, test scenarios, styling, and domain language live in your app’s repository.

Sixth pass, after the owner’s read of the positioning and values pages: Fablebook is “a UI workbench for Phoenix LiveView” everywhere, and the positioning is shorter (mock up all of your user flows and preview them with realistic data); the developer’s job is to mock up the app’s user flows and see how every screen will look, with setup as adding `fablebook` to mix.exs and mounting one dev route in Phoenix; the stakeholder job is to go through every user flow screen by screen, and the need is one catalog with share links for mockups and a scenario coverage map for blind spots; the assistants row promises LLM context for every user persona, JTBD, UI component and screen, with component styles as structured text; the Exact value drops the address, the Calm value says the UI catalog has neutral styling to keep the focus on the screens it shows, the Honest value says which screens are covered, and the claim that Fablebook never ships in a production build is gone from the values, the messaging pillars and the presence note; “ink on neutral” is “neutral” in plain statements.

Fifth pass, after the owner’s read of the audience table: the developer’s job is to mock up every screen and see how they will look in user flows, then keep refining; the setup says add Fablebook to Mix and mount one dev route in Phoenix; the stakeholder job is to go through all the user flows screen by screen and give feedback on whether they work for users; the stakeholder need is a catalog to preview all user flows in every scenario, links to share mockups for feedback and a coverage map; the coding assistants row promises full context (user personas, screens, user flows, UI conventions) and structured text for jobs to be done, domain language and UI component styles; “situations users meet” and “the dev routes block” are gone from every page; a Job to be done term joins the key terms.

Fourth pass, after the owner’s read of the positioning and values pages: the part of Fablebook you open is the “UI catalog” (the descriptor stays “a workbench for Phoenix LiveView UIs”); “canon” is “domain language”; “reviewer” and “library authors” are gone from the audience (designers, product people and other stakeholders; coding assistants and other LLM tools); the developer’s job reads “see how each one looks … until the whole UI is perfect”; the values say what they mean in plain words (a mockup that does not match production, “Card declined at send time” as the example name, which user flows and screens are covered, a Gap or a Waived mark with the reason); the same wording is swept through every page.

Third plain-language pass, after the owner’s read of the positioning and values pages: the developer’s job is now to mock up every screen of the app and keep refining until the whole UI is right (not “a screen”), and the phrases about the “host app’s own layout”, “renders through” and “real layout and CSS” are replaced by the plain point that you are previewing your real UI; the same wording is swept through the pillars, values, presence note, brand-color rule, glossary and captions.

Second plain-language pass, after the owner’s read of the summary page: the descriptor is now “A workbench for Phoenix LiveView UIs” (in full, “for user interfaces written in Phoenix LiveView”); the positioning, pitch, job, audience and boilerplate say what the product is for (mock up and iterate on a UI, see every screen in a user’s journey from the happy path to the edge cases) instead of “the happy one”, “the failed save” and “inside your own layout and styles”; the voice line is “Calm and plain” and says “user”, not “person”; the same wording is swept through every page and caption.

Plain-language pass: the tagline, positioning, pitch, audience, voice and glossary now speak in what a person using the app goes through (screens, paths, the happy path and what goes wrong) instead of “states”; the same wording is swept through every page, caption, the README, Hex page, social card and the mock command output.
First edition of this brand book: the logo (a lowercase f whose stem ends in a gilt bookmark ribbon), a light and a dark theme, an ink-on-neutral workbench, the docs and README looks, and the voice.

idea.line: A bookmark keeps your place in a book. A scenario keeps one screen in one case, ready to come back to.
explanation: Most UI work is judged on the happy path. The empty first visit, the failed payment and the client name that runs across three lines are where screens let users down, and finding them means clicking through the whole app. Fablebook shows each as a named scenario to open, compare and link to, so a team sees the whole user flow.

The mark is the first letter of the name, a lowercase f, whose stem becomes a bookmark ribbon with a swallowtail end, hanging below the baseline. The ribbon is the same shape the UI catalog uses to mark the current scenario. In the logo it is the one gilt piece: the place you’ve kept.

The f is the wordmark’s own f, from Schibsted Grotesk, cut once under the crossbar. Nothing in the mark is a shield, a lock or an eye. Fablebook helps people see what is there; it does not guard, watch or certify.

tagline: The whole journey, not just the happy path.
positioning: A UI catalog for Phoenix LiveView. Mock up all of your user flows and preview them with realistic data so you can quickly iterate to perfection. For developers, designers, product people and LLMs.
job: Help me mock up my app’s user flows, see how every screen will look, and keep refining until the whole UI is perfect.

audience.job: Mock up my app’s user flows and see how every screen will look. Then keep refining until the whole UI is perfect, from first idea to finished.

values.meaning: Previews your real UI, not a lookalike. A mockup that doesn’t match production gets you feedback on a screen your users will never see.
Names each scenario by the case it shows, like “Card declined at send time”. Never “variant 3”.

Says which screens are covered and which are not. “Gap” marks a case nobody has pictured; “Waived” marks one you chose to skip, with your reason.
Your user flows, test scenarios, styling, and domain language all live in your app’s repository.

presence.note: The UI catalog stays neutral on purpose, so your app’s own colors are the only color on screen.

logo.mark: The first letter of the name, a lowercase f. Its stem is cut once, a gap under the crossbar, and below the cut it becomes a bookmark ribbon in gilt: the same stem width, straight sides, a swallowtail end, hanging below the baseline. The f above the cut is the wordmark’s own f.
logo.wordmark: Fablebook, one word, in Schibsted Grotesk at weight 650, outlined from the font so no live text is needed. The ribbon is part of the word: it is the f. The other eight letters are the font’s, spaced by the font.
logo.together: The word and the ribbon are one drawing. Do not retype the name, separate the ribbon, or use the ribbon on its own as a bookmark icon.
logo.mono: One color is the same drawing in a single color: the gap under the crossbar and the notch carry the form, so nothing is redrawn. Ink on light, Vellum on dark.
logo.small: The logo has three cuts, drawn for their size. Display cut (49 px tall and up): Wide gap, long ribbon. Middle cut (25 to 48 px): Wider gap, longer ribbon and a deeper notch, at least 3 px. Small cut (24 px and below): The gap closes: the f and ribbon become one shape with a deep-notched foot. The app tile and the 16 and 32 px favicons use a heavier f (weight 800 at 32 px, 900 at 16 px) that fills the tile from top to bottom. The ribbon runs out through the bottom edge and its notch is cut through the tile, so the tile is not a plain light letter on a rounded square. Below 16 px, do not use the mark.
logo.clear: Keep clear space on every side equal to the height of the letter b (its ascender), measured from the outermost edge of the logo. Nothing enters it: no text, edge or other logo.
logo.minNote: On screen, the logo is never smaller than 14 px tall and the tile never smaller than 16 px. In print, never smaller than 12 mm wide.
logo.theme: The logo has a version for each theme. On light, the word is Ink and the ribbon is Gilt; on dark, the word is Vellum and the ribbon is Gilt Bright. Use the version made for the background; do not make one by inverting the other.
logo.background: No shape behind the logo: it sits directly on the page. The one derived exception is the app tile (favicon, app icon, avatar), where the f sits on a rounded Ink tile. A photograph or screenshot behind the logo needs a calm area at least as wide as the logo plus its clear space.
logo.florin: An f with a stem below the baseline can be read as ƒ, the function sign. Developers know it, and for a Phoenix library of function components it is an acceptable second reading. The name is also one letter from another well-known name, and a light f on a rounded square is a common app-icon pattern; the tile avoids it by running the ribbon through the bottom edge.
misuse: Don’t retype the name or stretch, squeeze or rotate the logo.
Don’t recolor the ribbon, or make the word gilt.
Don’t put a plate, badge or any shape behind the logo, except the app tile.
Don’t add the tagline, the descriptor or any text to the logo.
Don’t separate the ribbon and use it alone as a bookmark.
Don’t use the dark drawing on a light page, or the light drawing on a dark one.

useByOthers: Hex packages, blogs, newsletters and conference sites may use the logo unchanged to refer to Fablebook.

color.notes: Ratios are WCAG 2.2 contrast, computed from the hex values. A pair that passes here says nothing about a whole product built with it. Gilt on Paper is 3.4:1: enough for a shape, not for text. Hairline and Dim Line only divide; they are never the only boundary of a control.

name.descriptor: Call it “a UI catalog for Phoenix LiveView” and what it shows “scenarios”. Describe what it is for in the user’s terms: screens, user flows, the happy path, errors and edge cases, not “states” or “components” alone.

terms.meaning: What Fablebook is, and what you open in the browser: a sidebar, toolbar, inspector and palette around the canvas.
The words your team and users use for things in your app, such as invoice or plan, as structured text.
What a user is trying to get done, such as paying an invoice. Also called a JTBD.
The framed area where a scenario is shown: your real UI.
The catalog entry for one screen or component, its subject. It owns that subject’s scenarios.
One screen shown in one case, such as the invoice card for a new account. It has a clear name and a link you can share.
What a user is going through when they see a screen, such as “Empty: new account, nothing sent yet”. Kinds: happy path, empty, many, error, long.
Scenarios shown together in one grid for comparison. Each keeps its own address.
The inputs of a function component, in Phoenix’s own words.
A scenario shown with a value you changed in a control. Temporary: your code is untouched.
A note that a case is set aside on purpose, with your reason. It stays visible.
A case with no scenario and no waiver: nobody has pictured it yet.
One catalog with its own settings, mounted at one path. An app may have several.
The Phoenix app you are building, which Fablebook runs in during development.

A UI catalog for Phoenix LiveView: mock up all of your user flows and preview them with realistic data.

Fablebook is an open-source UI catalog for Phoenix LiveView. Mock up all of your user flows and preview them with realistic data, from the happy path to the edge cases, and see which cases nobody has covered yet.
Storybook for Phoenix, “knobs”, “variants”, “every state”, “blazing fast”, “seamless”, “powerful”. Fablebook shows cases; whether a screen is good is for your team to decide.

imagery.guidance: Fablebook’s pictures show the UI catalog at work with real labels: a story with its scenarios, a coverage map, and a command. They need no stock photography and no illustration.

show.subject: A coverage map
show.detail: Each story against each kind of case: a scenario, a waiver or a gap in every cell.

show.subject: A command
show.detail: A real command with its flags, in JetBrains Mono on the code ground.

never: A checkmark as proof a screen is done
imagery.why: Fablebook shows how a screen behaves from the happy path to the edge cases. These pictures say it tells stories, reviews design or guarantees quality, and Fablebook does none of those.
imagery.note: The pictures in this book are illustrations drawn from the UI catalog’s real labels and structure. They show the layout this book recommends, not screenshots of the current product, and the data in them is invented.

rules: No gilt in code, so nothing in code looks like the ribbon. The Gap brick appears only as the word “gap” in coverage output, where it means a gap.
Module names and function heads stand out by weight, not by another color.

Use these colors where Fablebook styles code: slides, social cards, blog posts and screenshots. GitHub and ExDoc color their own code; leave that alone.
Show code that matches the current release, not pseudo-code.

graphicElements.head: One shape that keeps your place: the ribbon.
graphicElements.intro: The ribbon is the brand’s only graphic device. It is the same shape as the stem of the logo: straight sides and a swallowtail end. It marks one thing per view, the place you are keeping, and it is the only gilt allowed inside the UI catalog.
items: A 4 px wide ribbon on the sidebar’s selected scenario and on the canvas frame’s top edge. In the UI catalog it is Ink, not gilt; on the docs site and in slides it may be gilt.
On the docs site, a gilt ribbon hangs from the top of a page you have bookmarked or are reading from a link. One per page, never decorative.
graphicElements.never: The ribbon never repeats as a pattern, never frames a block, never marks more than one item, and never stands in for the logo.

legal: Fablebook is open source. The logo and this brand book are covered by the repository’s license unless it says otherwise.
No trademark registration is claimed in this book, and none was searched. Use ™, not ®, only if the maintainers decide to claim the name.
Fonts are SIL Open Font License 1.1; the license texts are in the assets fonts folder.
contact: Questions about the brand and requests to use it: the Fablebook maintainers, through the project’s issue tracker.
Approval: the maintainers approve any use that changes the logo or colors; unchanged use under these rules needs no approval.

toReview.detail: The descriptor is “A UI catalog for Phoenix LiveView”, and the part you open is the same thing. “Workbench” is gone from the book.

toReview.choice: One word for each thing: scenario, case, story.
toReview.detail: A scenario is one screen in one case; a case is what a user is going through (a first visit, nothing there yet, an error). “Case” replaces “situation”, which read as a synonym of “scenario”; “condition” is the alternative. “Story” is still the word for one screen; if user flows are your unit, it changes with the glossary and coverage map.

toReview.choice: Edited is set apart from Gap and Waived.
toReview.detail: Edited is temporary, so it is a round outlined pill, listed apart from the two coverage marks. Gap is brick, not amber, which would read as gilt; Waived has a dashed outline. Meanings stay short until Fablebook is further along.

toReview.choice: The terminal prints the words gap and waived in color.
toReview.detail: Gap is brick and waived is slate; both are written out, so the table reads without color. It is the one place brick appears in code.

toReview.choice: The book says screens, paths and cases, not “states”.
toReview.detail: Scenario, story, gap, waived and edited are the product’s own words.

toReview.choice: Some audience promises are the owner’s wording.
toReview.detail: Previewing user flows with realistic data, a scenario coverage map, personas, jobs to be done, component styles as structured text, and “test scenarios” and “styling” in your repository are not confirmed as shipped.
“Canon” came from the product’s notes; confirm the name there. There is no draft label: the UI catalog has only Edited, Gap and Waived.

toReview.choice: The ribbon is part of the f.
toReview.detail: It is the f’s stem below one cut. A logo with a whole f and a ribbon beside it would state the initial twice.

toReview.choice: The name sits close to a very well-known one.
toReview.detail: Fablebook is one letter from a famous social network, whose icon is a lowercase f on a rounded tile. The tile’s ribbon runs out through the bottom edge to break that. Name clearance was not searched.

toReview.choice: Gilt is a docs-and-logo color only.
toReview.detail: The UI catalog has no accent. If it ever feels sterile, the ribbon on the current scenario is the first place to add gilt.
Docs, README and Hex render light by default, with a dark theme for dark devices. The UI catalog follows the device.

notChecked: Name and trademark clearance were not searched; the name was kept. Code samples follow the README and were not run. Logo legibility was checked on test sheets and by model readers, not with people. Contrast is computed for the pairs listed here, not for a whole product. Print color was not proofed. The favicon and tile were not checked on a real device or in Safari, and the 16 px tile still sits close to a plain letter on a rounded square.
retired: The plain bookmark ribbon on its own as the logo, which reads as a stock bookmark icon.
Any S, book or cover shape.
